new_statements.rule_in_words: Makhuwa (including the Tanzanian Ruvuma dialects Ikorovere and Imitthupi and Imeetto) is a restricted tone language: H tones are placed by morphology (verbs) or largely by noun class (nouns), with H-tone doubling in many dialects that is blocked phrase-finally and on the second mora of a phrase-penult bimoraic syllable. Vowel length is contrastive. No source examined says anything about word stress; the only accessible statement on penultimate prominence is van der Wal 2009: 20 (Enahara variant): 'Makhuwa does not have automatic penultimate lenghtening as in other Bantu languages, such as Makwe and Makonde.'
new_statements.exceptions: Tone: Imitthupi shifts some H tones one mora leftward; Imeetto and the Ruvuma dialects ban word-final underlying H (so the central-dialect penult/final H contrast in class 7/8 bimoraic stems does not exist there). Nothing on stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone-doubling restrictions are stated over the phonological phrase (phrase-final, phrase-penult), not the word. The absence-of-penultimate-lengthening statement (van der Wal 2009: 20, 34) concerns the Enahara variant, not Meetto; Devos 2013 repeats it second-hand for 'Makhuwa variants' citing Kisseberth.
new_statements.identity_note: Kisseberth 2003 draws its data from the Ikorovere (Tunduru) and Imitthupi (Masasi) dialects of southern Tanzania with explicit Imeetto comparisons; Glottolog assigns Hassan 2010 (Imithupi) and Ismail 2000 (Meto) to makh1261, so these Tanzanian 'Ruvuma' varieties fall under Makhuwa-Meetto, though Ikorovere's Glottolog assignment could not be confirmed (Glottolog reference search returned no results). Kröger & Iseminger 2009 is Meetto of Cabo Delgado (Balama). van der Wal 2009 describes Makhuwa-Enahara (Ilha de Moçambique), a different variety; its no-penultimate-lengthening statement is used only as a domain note. Meinhof 1908's informant was from Newala (north of the Ruvuma) = makh1261.

new_statements.quote: p. 270: "These vowels occur short or long, just as in Swahili and other Bantu languages, e and i are frequently interchanged, e.g., ipiro or epiro, a path." p. 290 (sec. 35, past tense): "The a of the third person singular (being really aa) has a stress which distinguishes it from the previous tense. In that tense the -ho- is emphasized." p. 292 (sec. 43, Past Conditional): "This tense is formed by inserting -a- between the verb and the personal prefix and changing the final -a into -ale, -ele, or -ile. The first syllable is stressed, and this distinguishes it from the relative. [...] katunale, watunale, atunale, natunale, mwatunale, atunale." (scanned shows 'kdtunale', 'dtunale', 'ndtunale', 'mwdtunale' = acute accent on the stressed a)

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's 'tone language, no stress statement' (Kisseberth 2003): Woodward never mentions tone and gives no stress placement rule; what he hears as 'stress' distinguishing the -aho- past 3sg and the Past Conditional from neighbouring tenses is a morphologically conditioned prominence on the tense-prefix vowel (long aa / acute-marked a), which later work (Cheng & Kisseberth 1979; Kisseberth 2003) treats as grammatical tone on verb prefixes. It neither agrees with nor contradicts a placement reading; it adds that the earliest Ruvuma-Makua description records prominence contrasts only on tense prefixes. Also confirms, via the vowel note, contrastive vowel length without any…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No general word-stress placement rule is given anywhere in the grammar. The phonology section (alphabet, p. 270-272) notes only that vowels are short or long and lists vowel assimilations. 'Stress' appears twice, and both times it is a grammatically conditioned prominence used to tell tenses apart: in the -aho- past tense the 3sg prefix a (underlying aa) 'has a stress', whereas in the preceding tense the -ho- syllable is emphasized (p. 290); in the Past Conditional (-a- + -ale/-ele/-ile) the first syllable (the prefix vowel a, marked with an acute) is stressed to distinguish it from the relative form (p. 292). These are contrasts on specific morphemes, not a rule for the word.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the only remarks are the two tense-specific contrasts quoted
new_statements.identity_note: Woodward 1926 describes the Makua of the Ruvuma district (UMCA Masasi mission field, Tanzania; 'the country.. on the Ruvuma, both above and below the Lujenda'), a revision of Maples 1879 from the same area; this is the Tanzanian Meetto/Kimakua zone = makh1261 and not the coastal Mozambican varieties (Woodward notes that the Maugham booklet 'is no help to one studying the language in the Ruvuma district'). The catalog's Kisseberth 2003 record draws on the Ikorovere (Tunduru) and Imitthupi (Masasi) dialects of the same region. Ismail 2000 (unopened) is titled for the 'Meto variety'.

sources.note: Nothing on stress or penultimate lengthening. Sec. 3.3 (pp. 551-552): contrastive long vowels, maximally bimoraic syllables. Sec. 3.4 Tone (pp. 553-555): no lexical tone contrasts in verbs; H tone assigned by morphology; tone doubling blocked phrase-finally and on the 2nd mora of a phrase-penult bimoraic syllable. Data dialects Ikorovere and Imitthupi (Tanzania) with explicit Imeetto comparisons.
